sections.h2: Selling a house in Cliffside Park, NJ
sections.html:
Cliffside Park is one of the most densely packed boroughs in New Jersey, so a sale here is often a condominium, a co-op unit or a house on a very small lot. The borough requires a certificate of continued occupancy for a sale, issued through its building department, and the deed is filed in Hackensack through the Bergen County Clerk.

This page walks through the local paperwork, the tax calendar and the Bergen County steps that apply when you sell.

The borough holds about 26,539 residents in under a square mile. The middle value of an owner-occupied home is $588,200, far above the national $332,700, and a little over half the homes (51.4%) are lived in by their owners. A seller with a condo, a rented unit or an inherited multifamily building is dealing with a different market than a suburban house seller.

sections.h2: Getting buyers: transit, views and listing details
sections.html:
Commuting is what many buyers ask about first. The average trip to work runs 35.5 minutes, well above the 26.4 minutes for the country as a whole. Anderson Avenue and Palisade Avenue carry most north-south traffic, and Palisade Avenue has views toward the Hudson River and the Manhattan skyline. NJ Transit bus lines 156, 159 and 181 go to Manhattan, the 22 serves Jersey City, and the 751 and 755 run locally.

About 65 percent of households speak a language other than English at home, so listing materials in more than one language can widen your buyer pool.

  • Name the bus line and the walking distance to it in your listing.
  • Photograph the view if you have one, and note which floor you are on.
  • For a condo or co-op, collect the association's budget and rules before the first showing.

sections.h2: Certificate of occupancy for a sale
sections.html:
The building department requires a Certificate of Occupancy for the sale of property. It is at the Municipal Complex, 525 Palisade Avenue, Room 220, phone 201-313-2042, with counter hours of 8:30 to 4:30. The applications page carries a form titled Certificate of Continued Occupancy for Sale, with a separate form for rentals.

After the inspections are done and the requirements are met, the Construction Code Official issues either a Certificate of Occupancy or a Certificate of Approval. The same office issues permits for alterations, demolitions and interior renovations, which means unpermitted work can come to light during a sale. Cash is no longer taken in any borough department, so plan to pay by check, debit or credit card.

The Planning Board sits on the first Monday of each month and the Board of Adjustment on the fourth, which matters if you need a variance before selling. Ask the department for the current fee for the sale certificate before you file.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and where to pay
sections.html:
Real estate tax is collected in four installments, due the first of February, May, August and November. The tax collector sits on the second floor of 525 Palisade Avenue, phone 201-313-2050. You can pay through the borough's online lookup page, mail a check to the Tax Collector at that address, or use the drop box by the Borough Hall entrance.

Taxes here run modest for Bergen County. A borough release put the average residence at an assessed $373,110 with a yearly bill of $9,982, ninth lowest of the county's 70 municipalities. That figure is from an earlier year, so rely on your own current bill for closing math.

For state relief programs, start at the Division of Taxation's relief page. Selling while you collect a homestead benefit? Say so on the application, or take the benefit as a credit at closing. If you do neither, it goes toward the new owner's taxes.

sections.h2: How to appeal your assessment before selling
sections.html:
Tax appeals are filed with the Bergen County Board of Taxation in Hackensack, and the calendar is tight: April 1, or May 1 following a revaluation. The board encourages online filing and can be reached at 201-336-6300. Start with the borough assessor at 201-313-2009, whose office also defends appeals.

The board starts from the assumption that your assessment is right. To change that you need proof it exceeds market value, and proof means recent comparable sales rather than frustration over the bill. Any savings mostly go to whoever owns the unit after the ruling, so talk to your attorney before filing on a property you are about to sell.

  • Compare your assessment with recent sales of similar units in your building or block.
  • Check that the assessor shows the correct square footage and unit count.
  • Ask whether a pending appeal could affect the closing adjustments.

sections.h2: Deed filing, transfer fees and income tax forms
sections.html:
Deeds, mortgages and liens for the county are recorded by the Bergen County Clerk. Sellers pay the state realty transfer fee. On residential and cooperative-unit deeds over $1,000,000 an extra graduated fee kicks in, starting at 1 percent of the price between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000 and climbing to 3.5 percent above $3,500,000. With a middle value of $588,200, most Cliffside Park sales land under that line, but a penthouse or a multifamily building can cross it. The buyer pays a separate 1 percent fee on certain purchases above $1 million.

At closing the seller hands over a gross income tax form. Residents of New Jersey sign a residency certification, while an owner who has moved out of state prepays estimated income tax, figured at either two percent of the price or the 8.97 percent rate on the gain. On the federal side, the rule for a principal residence can shelter $250,000 of profit, or $500,000 for a married couple.

sections.h2: Which routes sell a Cliffside Park home fastest?
sections.html:
Two routes move fastest: an investor purchase, or a well-priced listing with the certificate already in hand. A unit with a clean inspection history and complete association paperwork leaves a buyer fewer open questions.

If you inherited a unit, have tenants or owe back taxes, get permit status and a tax payoff in writing before you accept an offer. An as-is buyer will still need the occupancy certificate and a clear deed, so put those items on your checklist whichever route you choose.

A short to-do order keeps a Cliffside Park sale moving: call the building department about the sale certificate, ask the tax collector for a payoff or current balance, gather association documents if the unit is a condo or co-op, and have your attorney or title agent order the deed work. Selling for cash removes the buyer's mortgage underwriting and appraisal, two common sources of delay. The occupancy certificate and the deed filing still happen.

faqs.q: Is a certificate required to sell in Cliffside Park?
faqs.a: Yes. The borough building department requires a Certificate of Occupancy for the sale of property, and its applications page carries a separate sale form.

faqs.q: Where is the Cliffside Park sale certificate filed?
faqs.a: At the building department, Municipal Complex, 525 Palisade Avenue, Room 220, or by phone at 201-313-2042. The borough accepts check, debit or credit card, not cash.

faqs.q: What are the Cliffside Park tax installment dates?
faqs.a: The first of February, May, August and November. You can pay online, by mail, or in the drop box by the Borough Hall entrance.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my Cliffside Park assessment?
faqs.a: Appeals are due April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation, to the Bergen County Board of Taxation. Call the borough assessor first to review your numbers.

faqs.q: Which office records a Cliffside Park deed?
faqs.a: The Bergen County Clerk in Hackensack files deeds and mortgages for the borough, usually through your attorney or title agent along with the state fee and income tax forms.
